title: AI-Driven SOC: Why Southeast Asian Enterprises Can’t Wait
summary: Discover why Southeast Asian enterprises need AI-driven SOC operations to close the 29-minute breakout gap. Learn more with Concentrix.
body_markdown:
Ask most SOC vendors what’s wrong with security operations and they’ll describe a story about sophisticated attackers outsmarting legacy tools. That’s not really it. The real problem is arithmetic. A typical four-analyst SOC works through 300 to 400 high-fidelity alerts a week, roughly 90% of them benign \[1\]. Somebody still has to look at every one before anyone can say which is which, and nobody’s found a way to add more hours to the day to make that math work.


Manual triage was built for an attacker who took hours, sometimes days, to move. That attacker is gone. Southeast Asia, in particular, doesn’t have the option of simply hiring its way out of the gap.


## Why the Traditional SOC Model Is Breaking


Here’s the number that should worry you more than any vendor pitch: the average time between an attacker’s first foothold and their first lateral move fell to 29 minutes in 2025, down 65% from the year before. The fastest recorded breakout was 27 seconds\[2\]. A financial platform in Singapore, an e-commerce operation in Thailand, a logistics network in Indonesia, none of them get 29 minutes of grace if their SOC is still running on human speed.


Then there’s the noise problem, which is arguably worse. Close to half of everything a SOC sees is a false positive, and the average enterprise now manages nearly 11 separate security consoles just to keep watch \[3\]. Every hour an analyst spends chasing a false alarm is an hour they’re not spending on the 29 minutes that actually count.


Southeast Asia carries an extra burden here, and it’s the part most vendor pitches skip. The global cybersecurity workforce gap sits at roughly 4.8 million unfilled roles\[4\], and across Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Indonesia, more than 90% of organisations say they’ve had at least one breach they attribute in part to the skills shortage\[5\]. Malaysia’s government took this seriously enough to launch a national Cyber Security Academy in 2025\[5\]. Your problem was never really that you needed a smarter tool. It’s that you needed people who don’t exist yet, in a market that isn’t producing them fast enough.


## What ‘AI-Driven’ Actually Means


Every vendor calls their product agentic now, the same way everyone called their product AI-powered in 2023. Most of what ships under that label is still a decision tree with better marketing. The real distinction is worth knowing. Old SOAR ran on rigid if-then logic: fast, but blind to anything it wasn’t scripted for. Genuinely agentic AI reasons through a case the way a decent analyst would, correlating signals, testing hypotheses against something like MITRE ATT&CK, and adjusting its approach as the evidence changes. It isn’t following a script. It’s building one, in real time, per case.


What that buys you, practically, is an AI agent doing the enrichment, the correlation, and the first draft of the investigation narrative, so your analysts spend their day reviewing verdicts and making calls instead of drowning in raw alerts. Nobody’s job disappears. What changes is where the hours go, which is worth saying plainly if you’re the one signing off on the budget.


## Build or Outsource? An Honest Answer


Running a genuine 24/7 SOC in-house costs somewhere between $1.5 million and $2.9 million a year once staffing, tooling, and overhead are accounted for\[6\], and the expensive part was never the tooling. It’s finding and keeping the people. Given the talent shortage above, that math gets harder in Southeast Asia than it does in markets with a deeper bench to draw from.


Call it build versus partner rather than build versus buy. Building buys you control. Partnering buys you speed and access to people you probably can’t hire yourself right now. If you go the partner route, don’t take the pitch at face value: ask for actual analyst headcount, shift coverage, and real MTTD and MTTR numbers. Plenty of vendors say agentic in their marketing. Fewer have actually built it.


## Twenty-Nine Minutes and Counting


Twenty-nine minutes isn’t a marketing number. It’s the actual amount of time you have, and CrowdStrike’s data shows it getting shorter every year they measure it. Whatever you decide, build, partner, or some mix of both, the decision needs to account for that number, not the org chart you inherited two years ago.


This is the kind of work we help with at Concentrix: building SOC operations around AI from day one instead of bolting it onto something older. The gap between a 29-minute attacker and an hours-long response doesn’t close by itself, and waiting for a breach to force the decision is the expensive way to learn that.


**Sources:**


*\[1\] **** Prophet Security, industry analysis of SOC alert volume: a four-analyst SOC investigating 300-400 high-fidelity alerts weekly, approximately 90% resolving as benign.*


*\[2\] **** CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report: average eCrime breakout time and fastest recorded breakout.*


*\[3\] **** Microsoft/Omdia State of the SOC 2026 report: false positive rate and average security console count.*


*\[4\] **** ISC2 Cybersecurity Workforce Study: global cybersecurity workforce gap.*


*\[5\] **** Statement from Fortinet’s Southeast Asia leadership, as reported by Cyber Security Asia (Feb 2025): breach attribution across Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Indonesia, and Malaysia’s Cyber Security Academy launch.*


*\[6\] **** Industry benchmarks for 24/7 in-house SOC operating costs (Ponemon Institute; Expel; Netsurion, 2026).*
